tier_reason: First-party blog table (CRC32 of 1 GByte, Core i7 860, GCC 4.7 vs Visual C++ 2010) measured with public benchmark code (Crc32Test.cpp in the repo, which times crc32_1byte against crc32_4bytes/8bytes/16bytes). It is not A for two reasons: the flags used for the 2011-2015 table are never stated (the repo Makefile with -O3 was only added in 2016), and the baseline that was measured is the author's own Sarwate byte-table reimplementation, not zlib's crc32().

corrections.baseline: Classic byte-wise Sarwate table-lookup CRC32 (the author's own crc32_1byte reimplementation). The page says zlib and PHP use this algorithm, but zlib's crc32() itself is not benchmarked.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Core i7 860, CRC32 of 1 GByte, figures given as GCC 4.7 / Visual C++ 2010: Slicing-by-8 1800 / 1400 MByte/s; Slicing-by-16 3000 / 2000 MByte/s; Slicing-by-16 4x unrolled with prefetch 3200 / 2000 MByte/s; Slicing-by-4 1050 / 840 MByte/s. The standard Sarwate byte-table implementation runs at 375 MByte/s, so Slicing-by-8 and Slicing-by-16 are about 3.7-8.5x faster than it, and Slicing-by-4 about 2.2-2.8x (derived from page data). The original bitwise version runs at 35 MByte/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.7 and Visual C++ 2010. For VC++ the page only says 'full optimization is enabled', and it mentions that GCC -O2 and up unrolls the loop. Exact flags for the published table are not stated. The repo Makefile, added in 2016 after the measurements, uses -O3 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -s.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is a textbook Sarwate byte-table loop, not real zlib. zlib's crc32() has processed four bytes at a time since 1.2.0 in 2003 (the BYFOUR code from Rodney Brown, similar to slicing-by-4, which this page measures at 840-1050 MByte/s). Since 1.2.12 in 2022 zlib uses braided CRC, which its ChangeLog says is 1.5-3x faster again. The speedup over an actual zlib build is therefore much smaller than 3.7-8.5x, and it was never measured. Hardware and compilers are from 2011-2015 (Core i7 860, GCC 4.7, VC++ 2010). There is no PCLMUL/SIMD path, so modern implementations such as zlib-ng and Chromium's zlib are faster. There have been no commits since 2021-09-29.

notes: Numbers on the page match the record, except that the record's lower ratio bound (~4.3x) is wrong: 1400/375 is about 3.7x, and the record left out the VC++ Slicing-by-16 figure of 2000 MByte/s. Metadata checked via gh: Zlib license, 194 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2021-09-29, so abandoned. The main correction is the baseline: the page equates Sarwate with zlib, but zlib's crc32() has not been byte-wise Sarwate since 2003.
